# JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

Xudong Wu Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong   
Guangchen Lan Affiliation: Salesforce AI Research    Mingqi Yuan
Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong    Jiayu Chen
Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Correspondence to:
<jiayuc@hku.hk>

###### Abstract

The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and
the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other
component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive
alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the
model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and
may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation.
To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce
JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an
executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through
reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and
harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the
evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and
reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime
improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs
recursive self-improvement (RSI).

###### Keywords: 

multi-agent reinforcement learning, language agents, joint
harness–weight optimization

## 1 Introduction

A language agent consists of a model and a harness. The model weights
determine its learned reasoning and decision-making capabilities, while
the harness organizes how these capabilities are used. Improving an
agent therefore admits two complementary paths: training its model
weights and improving its harness.

Existing methods have made progress along both paths. Reinforcement
learning methods train model weights from task feedback, improving the
policy that makes decisions ([Yu et al., 2022](#bib.bib8); [Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21)). Alternatively, harness optimization changes the
runtime surrounding the model ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Shao et
al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). However, agent performance depends jointly on
both components, and optimizing either alone can leave overall gains
constrained by the other. The comparison with weight-only and
harness-only training in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")
further motivates learning model weights and harnesses together.

However, naively alternating updates to model weights and the harness
does not ensure their compatibility. As the model changes, an existing
harness may provide outdated or incorrect guidance that interferes with
task execution and limits performance gains. Such guidance also shapes
the experience used for training and may steer subsequent model updates
toward less effective behavior, potentially worsening performance over
time. We diagnose these issues through controlled comparisons and
failure trajectory analysis in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning").

WHALE mitigates this issue through small alternating updates to model
weights and harnesses. Its published instantiation updates model weights
through online rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RSFT) rather than RL, and
uses Meta-Harness search driven by a fixed external proprietary frontier
model ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). However, harness optimization
continues to rely on a fixed external proprietary frontier model to
propose improvements. Execution feedback guides harness selection, but
does not update the proposer itself. The capability to improve the
harness therefore remains delegated to an external model rather than
trained within the system. This motivates a different approach: making
harness generation a trainable policy and using the same task execution
outcome to train both the harness generator and the task performer.

We instantiate recursive self-improvement (RSI) by learning both task
execution and harness construction from the system’s own generated
programs, trajectories, and execution feedback. Harness-R1 supports the
potential of this direction: its trained harness Engineer outperforms
the evaluated fixed frontier editors, including proprietary models
([Shao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). However, it keeps the task-performing
model frozen during Engineer training. This leaves an open question:

How can both policies improve through reinforcement learning from their
shared task executions?

A natural starting point is to alternate updates to the two policies
using task outcomes. Yet alternation alone does not ensure that their
improvements remain compatible. We investigate this problem through
controlled diagnosis of a long-phase alternating run in which
performance initially improves and subsequently deteriorates
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
By evaluating saved model checkpoints with and without the same fixed
harness, we distinguish two sources of decline: the task-performing
model loses ability, and the unchanged harness becomes more harmful as
the model changes. In one task, a later model succeeds in 14 turns
without a harness but reaches the 50-turn limit under the old harness
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")b).
These findings motivate coordinating the two learners throughout
training, rather than relying on alternation alone.

We introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly
train a harness-generation policy and a task-execution policy through
reinforcement learning. We call the two policies the Engineer and the
Solver. The Engineer generates an executable harness, and the Solver
interacts with the environment under that harness. The generated program
and its multi-turn execution form a paired training example
(Figure [3](#S0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
The shared task outcome trains both policies, each on its own generated
tokens. Therefore, JoMoHa implements RSI: the improvement policy itself
learns from execution feedback, alongside the task-performing policy. We
release our code at
[https://github.com/xudongwu-0/coevolve](https://github.com/xudongwu-0/coevolve).

We evaluate JoMoHa on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, where it achieves
the highest success rates among the evaluated methods: 97.0%, 45.8%, and
68.0%, respectively
(Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Main Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning"),
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Schedule: give the Solver additional adaptation. ‣ 5.3 Coordinating Policy Updates ‣ 5 JoMoHa ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).

To coordinate the Engineer and Solver, JoMoHa combines
collaboration-aware value estimation, role-specific return
normalization, partner-trajectory weighting, and asymmetric update
schedules. We examine these design choices through component studies in
Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning").

Our contributions are threefold:

1.  1.  Diagnosing failure in alternating training. Fixed-component tests
        distinguish declining Solver capability from worsening harness
        compatibility. Trajectory analysis reveals how incorrect harness
        state disrupts otherwise successful execution. Together, these
        findings highlight risks to both task execution and continued
        learning, motivating compatibility-aware joint training.
2.  2.  Joint model–harness reinforcement learning. We introduce, to our
        knowledge, the first framework to jointly train an
        executable-harness generation policy and a task-execution policy
        through RL. The Engineer and Solver learn from the same task
        outcome, making both harness construction and task execution
        trainable within a shared learning process.
3.  3.  Coordination adaptations and empirical evaluation. We adapt
        cooperative-learning mechanisms to the Engineer–Solver setting and
        evaluate JoMoHa across three environments. Frozen-Engineer controls,
        fixed-Solver harness comparisons, and component studies assess the
        benefits of training the Engineer, improving the harness, and
        coordinating the two policies.

## 2 Related Work

#### Model-weight optimization.

Reinforcement learning improves language-model reasoning and
decision-making from task feedback ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)).
Single-Rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) uses one rollout per
prompt, a learned value model, and token-level calibration to stabilize
asynchronous agentic RL ([Hou et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). For tool-using
agents, Search-R1 learns when and how to retrieve information ([Jin et
al., 2025](#bib.bib18)), while ReTool learns to interleave reasoning
with code execution ([Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). RAGEN studies the
training dynamics of multi-turn agents ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20)). These methods improve the task-performing policy
under a prescribed runtime, rather than jointly learning a separate
policy that constructs that runtime. JoMoHa trains the Solver alongside
an Engineer whose generated harness shapes the Solver’s execution.

#### Harness optimization.

A complementary line improves the system surrounding the model. ReAct
organizes reasoning and action, while Self-Refine and Reflexion use
textual feedback to revise behavior ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib7);
[Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib12); [Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)).
OPRO and DSPy support instruction and pipeline optimization ([Yang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Khattab et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)). ADAS and
AFlow search over agent architectures and executable workflows ([Hu et
al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), and
Meta-Harness searches executable harnesses using prior code, scores, and
execution traces ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)). These approaches
motivate treating the runtime as an optimization object, but improving a
program does not necessarily train its generator. Harness-R1 makes
runtime editing a learned capability by training an Engineer through RL
against a frozen target agent ([Shao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). JoMoHa
further trains the Solver alongside the Engineer, allowing both policies
to adapt to their changing partner.

#### Joint learning and coordination.

WHALE jointly improves model weights and harnesses through alternating
updates ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). Its published instantiation
combines online RSFT with Meta-Harness search driven by a fixed external
proprietary frontier model. Compared with WHALE, JoMoHa learns the
harness-generating policy itself and trains both policies through RL
from the same executed program–rollout pair
(Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Joint learning and coordination. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).

Cooperative RL provides foundations for learning from team outcomes ([Yu
et al., 2022](#bib.bib8); [Foerster et al., 2017a](#bib.bib23); [Kuba et
al., 2021](#bib.bib24); [Foerster et al., 2017b](#bib.bib22); [van
Hasselt et al., 2016](#bib.bib25)). These classical methods were
primarily developed and evaluated in non-language environments. Adapting
these ideas to LLM training, particularly our program-mediated setting,
is nontrivial: the Engineer and Solver have separate token histories and
different decision horizons, while the Engineer’s program shapes the
Solver’s entire multi-turn rollout. Their execution conditions also
change as both policies learn. Our adaptations address critic
information, role-specific return scales, partner-trajectory weighting,
and update frequency. Component studies examine their contributions in
this setting, and the complete coordination design improves performance
over the Joint-only baseline
(Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).

| Method             | Harness adaptation | Engineer | Solver |
| ------------------ | ------------------ | -------- | ------ |
| Search-R1 / ReTool | Prescribed         | –        | RL     |
| Meta-Harness       | Code search        | External | Fixed  |
| Harness-R1         | Learned edits      | RL       | Fixed  |
| WHALE              | Code search        | External | RSFT   |
| JoMoHa             | Learned generation | RL       | RL     |

Table 1: Comparison of model–harness learning procedures. Engineer and
Solver columns describe parameter updates. A fixed Engineer can still
search for new harnesses. For Harness-R1, the Solver is frozen during
Engineer training. A dash denotes no separate harness Engineer.

## 3 Background

Reinforcement learning (RL) improves a policy, a distribution over
actions, through interaction and reward ([Sutton and Barto,
2018](#bib.bib11)). A Markov decision process (MDP) describes this
interaction using states, actions, transition dynamics, and rewards: the
next state depends on the current state and action. An episode is one
task attempt. Language agents observe only part of the environment, so
their policies use the available history. An _actor_ is the trainable
policy; a _critic_ predicts its future return and provides a baseline
for advantages—whether an outcome is better or worse than expected.

For a task $`x`$, the Engineer uses evidence $`e`$ to sample a proposal
trajectory $`\tau_{\mathrm{E}}`$. Validation and fallback map it to the
executed harness $`h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}})`$. The Solver acts
under $`h`$, producing trajectory $`\tau_{\mathrm{S}}`$ and terminal
task reward $`R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}})`$. For role
$`i\in\{\mathrm{E},\mathrm{S}\}`$, $`\theta_{i}`$ and $`\phi_{i}`$ are
actor and critic parameters, with actor policy $`\pi_{\theta_{i}}`$.
Indices $`t`$, $`b`$, and $`k`$ denote generated-token positions, paired
episodes, and saved checkpoints, respectively;
$`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(k)}`$ and $`h_{k}`$ identify saved weights and
code. The no-harness condition $`\varnothing`$ retains the base
executor.

SAO learns from one rollout per prompt using a critic ([Hou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)). Both roles share the task reward, while their
returns also include role-specific KL penalties that restrain divergence
from fixed reference policies.

## 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together?

We examine an alternating-training baseline that updates the Solver and
Engineer in separate phases. Such training may lead to over-adaptation
between the Solver and its harness: each component adapts to a
counterpart that subsequently changes, potentially making their learned
behavior less compatible. On ALFWorld, this baseline initially improves
from 83.0% to 90.5%, but then deteriorates across successive stages to
31.5%
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
In comparison, JoMoHa reaches 97.0%. We analyze the alternating run to
investigate how harness mismatch can affect both task execution and
Solver learning.

| Training scheme      | Checkpoint                          | Success (%) |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------- |
| Alternating training | $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(0)},h_{0}`$ | 83.0        |
|                      | $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(1)},h_{1}`$ | 90.5        |
|                      | $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)},h_{2}`$ | 78.5        |
|                      | $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)},h_{3}`$ | 48.5        |
|                      | $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(4)},h_{4}`$ | 31.5        |
| JoMoHa               | 144 rounds                          | 97.0        |

Table 2: Performance degradation during alternating training on
ALFWorld. Each alternating stage uses its corresponding Solver–harness
pair $`(\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(k)},h_{k})`$. The highest
alternating-stage success and the result of JoMoHa are bolded. The
fixed-code diagnosis is reported in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility

The stage-level results alone cannot distinguish declining Solver
ability from worsening harness compatibility, because both components
change across stages. We therefore hold one harness fixed and evaluate
it with different Solver checkpoints.

The percentage success $`\mathrm{SR}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},h)`$ evaluates
fixed Solver weights under a saved harness. The no-harness condition
$`h=\varnothing`$ removes the learned harness while retaining the base
executor. The harness contribution to a fixed Solver is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\Delta_{h}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},h)=\mathrm{SR}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},h)-\mathrm{SR}(\theta_{\mathrm{S}},\varnothing).
``` |  | (1) |

This comparison separates Solver performance without the learned harness
from the harness’s immediate effect on execution.

Specifically, we select earlier Solver weights
$`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)}`$, later weights
$`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}`$, and the saved harness $`h_{2}`$ from the
alternating run. For each Solver, we evaluate the same fixed harness and
the no-harness condition on the same ALFWorld evaluation tasks. The
following aggregate comparisons and trajectory analyses examine both
execution interference and Solver degradation.

(a) Aggregate success (%)

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Solver | No harness | Fixed $`h_{2}`$ | Harness effect |
| Earlier $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)}`$ | 82.5 | 78.5 | $`-4.0`$ |
| Later $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}`$ | 48.0 | 31.0 | $`-17.0`$ |
| Change | $`-34.5`$ | $`-47.5`$ | $`-13.0`$ |

(b) Case 1: Clean sponge and place on cart

| Solver | No harness | Fixed $`h_{2}`$ |
|----|----|----|
| Earlier $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)}`$ |  Success 16 turns |  Success 14 turns |
| Later $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}`$ |  Success 14 turns |  Timeout 50 turns |

Table 3: Execution interference and Solver degradation during
alternating training. (a) Aggregate success rates; harness effect is the
difference within each row in percentage points. (b) Case 1 from the
ALFWorld trajectory analysis: outcomes and episode lengths across four
Solver–harness combinations. Both $`h_{2}`$ conditions execute the
identical saved harness. No harness retains the base executor but
removes the learned harness.

#### Separating execution interference from Solver degradation.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")
reveals two distinct changes. Across each row, adding the same harness
reduces success by 4.0 points for $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(2)}`$ but 17.0
points for $`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}`$: its negative effect increases
by 13.0 points. Down the no-harness column, success falls from 82.5% to
48.0%: the Solver loses 34.5 points even when the learned harness is
removed. Together, these account for the decline under the fixed
harness:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\underbrace{-47.5}_{\text{system decline}}=\underbrace{-34.5}_{\text{Solver decline}}+\underbrace{-13.0}_{\text{compatibility loss}}.
``` |  | (2) |

The first comparison shows that an unchanged harness can increasingly
interfere with execution as the Solver changes. The additional loss
cannot be explained by the Engineer generating a worse new harness. At
$`\theta_{\mathrm{S}}^{(3)}`$, adding $`h_{2}`$ changes success to
failure on 18.0% of evaluation tasks and failure to success on 1.0%.

The second comparison shows that removing the harness does not restore
the later Solver’s earlier performance. The decline therefore extends
beyond interference during the current execution. It is consistent with
the concern that training under mismatched harnesses may steer the
Solver toward less effective behavior. These findings motivate
maintaining Solver–harness compatibility throughout training, rather
than treating the harness only as an inference-time aid.

#### Case 1: Harness-induced failure on ALFWorld.

We examine evaluation trajectories produced by the earlier and later
Solver checkpoints from the alternating training run analyzed above. The
task requires cleaning a sponge and placing it on a cart. The later
Solver succeeds in 14 turns without the learned harness, but reaches the
50-turn limit under the old harness $`h_{2}`$
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")b).
The earlier Solver succeeds in both conditions, taking 16 and 14 turns,
respectively. The later Solver therefore retains the behavior needed to
complete this task; the failure appears when it is combined with the old
harness.

The trajectory analysis reveals the following failure sequence:

1.  1.
    The environment advances. Cleaning has completed, so the remaining
    work is to finish navigation and placement.
2.  2.
    The harness fails to update its state. The executed action is stored
    in a nested field, but the old lookup uses a literal dotted key. The
    correct access is on the first line below; the old lookup is on the
    second:

    ``` ltx_verbatim
    ctx["action"]["final_action"]
    ctx.get("action.final_action")
    ```

    A dotted string is a different dictionary key, not a nested lookup,
    so the completed action is missed. A second state update can also
    overwrite earlier inventory evidence when the current observation
    omits the word indicating cleaning.
3.  3.
    Stale guidance sends execution backward. Although the environment
    has confirmed cleaning, the harness continues directing the Solver
    to find and clean the object. The episode loops through navigation
    and reaches the turn limit.

#### Case 2: Solver failure without the learned harness.

A contrasting ALFWorld case from the same training run exposes a failure
in the no-harness condition. After cleaning a potato and navigating to
the destination, the later Solver omits the final placement action and
eventually reaches the turn limit. Because no learned harness is active,
this failure cannot be attributed to interference from $`h_{2}`$. It
illustrates why removing an incompatible harness alone cannot address
all failures of the trained Solver.

### 4.2 From Compatibility to Coordinated Learning

Taken together, these findings suggest that a mismatched harness can
impair current task execution and may also distort the experience from
which the Solver learns. This creates a risk of a negative feedback loop
in which ineffective harness guidance and declining Solver capability
reinforce one another. Maintaining a compatible Solver–harness pair
throughout learning is therefore important.

Our unit of learning is a complete task attempt: the generated harness,
the actions taken under it, and the final outcome. The Engineer learns
to generate effective harnesses, while the Solver learns to complete
tasks under them. To mitigate this risk, our method uses their shared
task outcome to coordinate value estimation and policy updates,
supporting the joint adaptation of both policies.

## 5 JoMoHa

JoMoHa jointly trains two LLM policies: an Engineer that generates a
harness and a Solver that performs tasks under it. Both learn from the
outcome of the same task attempt
(Figure [3](#S0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
To coordinate their learning, we use collaboration-aware value
estimation, role-specific return normalization, partner-trajectory
weighting, and asymmetric update schedules.

### 5.1 Learning from a Shared Task Outcome

For a task $`x`$, the Engineer receives historical feedback $`e`$ and
samples a proposal trajectory $`\tau_{\mathrm{E}}`$. Validation and
fallback map that proposal to the executed harness
$`h=\mathcal{V}(\tau_{\mathrm{E}})`$. The Solver then interacts with the
environment under $`h`$, producing trajectory $`\tau_{\mathrm{S}}`$ and
task reward $`R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}})`$. An invalid proposal maps to
$`h=\varnothing`$, retaining the base executor.

The two policies share the objective

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(\theta_{\mathrm{E}},\theta_{\mathrm{S}})=\mathbb{E}_{x,e,h,\tau_{\mathrm{S}}}\left[R(x,\tau_{\mathrm{S}})\right],
``` |  | (3) |

where $`h`$ is the validation/fallback result and $`\tau_{\mathrm{S}}`$
is collected by the Solver under that harness. The task reward is binary
on ALFWorld.

The same reward trains both policies: the Engineer learns which
harnesses support successful execution, while the Solver learns how to
complete tasks under those harnesses. Each policy is updated on its own
generated outputs, without differentiating through harness execution. We
use a KL-regularized SAO-based actor–critic backbone ([Hou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)), with a fixed reference policy for each role. The
local realization retains behavior–proximal token-ratio decoupling.

### 5.2 Value Estimation for Two Different Roles

Each policy has an independent critic that estimates its expected
return, including task rewards and its own KL penalty. The critics
provide baselines for computing advantages: whether an outcome is better
or worse than expected.

#### Context: account for collaboration conditions.

The usefulness of an Engineer proposal depends on the Solver, while the
Solver’s performance depends on the harness. A critic
$`V_{\phi_{i}}(z_{i,t},c_{i})`$ predicts the role’s expected remaining
regularized return from its current history $`z_{i,t}`$ and a short
collaboration summary $`c_{i}`$. The supplemental fields describe the
task identifier, training version, and role-specific execution
conditions. The task field is a path or identifier, not a full
environment observation. Context is provided only to the critics and
does not change the actors’ inputs.

#### ValueNorm: account for different return scales.

The Engineer generates a harness once, whereas the Solver acts over
multiple turns. Their different output lengths and KL penalties can
produce different return scales despite the shared task reward. Writing
the raw, unweighted critic target as $`G_{i,t}`$, we normalize critic
targets separately for each role:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{i,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{G_{i,t}-m_{i}}{\sigma_{i}},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle V_{\phi_{i}}(z_{i,t},c_{i})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sigma_{i}\widehat{V}_{\phi_{i}}(z_{i,t},c_{i})+m_{i},`$ |  | (4) |

where $`m_{i}`$ and $`\sigma_{i}>0`$ are running return statistics.
Values are restored to their original scale before advantages are
computed. Hats denote normalized targets and predictions. This
critic-target normalization is separate from standardizing actor
advantages.

### 5.3 Coordinating Policy Updates

We compute advantages using generalized advantage estimation ([Schulman
et al., 2016](#bib.bib9)) and standardize them separately for the two
policies. We introduce two additional mechanisms to account for the
changing partner and the different adaptation needs of the two roles.

#### Peer: weight experience using the partner’s trajectory.

As both policies change, a recorded task attempt may become more or less
representative of their current collaboration. Peer adjusts its
influence using the paired partner trajectory:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{E},b,t}=w_{\mathrm{S},b}\bar{A}_{\mathrm{E},b,t},\qquad\widetilde{A}_{\mathrm{S},b,t}=w_{\mathrm{E},b}\bar{A}_{\mathrm{S},b,t},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\bar{A}_{i,b,t}`$ is the role-standardized advantage. Each
partner weight compares the likelihood of the recorded trajectory under
the policy snapshot used for the current update with its likelihood when
collected. We bound the weight to $`[0.5,2]`$, treat it as a constant
during optimization, and leave critic targets unchanged.

#### Schedule: give the Solver additional adaptation.

Changing the Engineer changes the harnesses under which the Solver
learns. To give the Solver additional adaptation without another
Engineer update, the coordination study repeats *joint, joint,
Solver-only* rounds. The resulting update ratio is Engineer:Solver
$`=2:3`$.

Solver-only rounds freeze the Engineer’s parameters but still sample
fresh harnesses. They use unit partner weights. Thus, the Solver
continues learning under sampled harnesses while their generating policy
remains fixed.

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Schedule: give the Solver additional adaptation. ‣ 5.3 Coordinating Policy Updates ‣ 5 JoMoHa ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")
summarizes the procedure. At deployment, we select a saved harness and
evaluate it with a frozen Solver checkpoint.

0:  Engineer and Solver policies, independent critics, reference
policies, task/evidence stream

1:  for each training round do

2:   Choose active roles according to Schedule.

3:   Engineer samples a code proposal from historical feedback.

4:   Validate it to obtain the executed harness and run the Solver.

5:   Record both outputs and their shared task reward.

6:   for each active role do

7:    Estimate values using Context and ValueNorm.

8:    Compute and standardize advantages.

9:    Apply Peer weights and update the actor through the SAO-based
path.

10:    Update the critic on normalized return targets.

11:   end for

12:  end for

13:  Select a saved harness and Solver checkpoint for evaluation.

Algorithm 1 Joint learning of the Engineer and Solver

## 6 Experiments

#### Experimental setup.

We evaluate JoMoHa on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, which test
household task completion, goal-directed shopping, and database
interaction, respectively ([Shridhar et al., 2021](#bib.bib4); [Yao et
al., 2022](#bib.bib5); [Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)). We report success
rates in all three environments, a separate WebShop score, and the
equally weighted mean of the three success rates. The ALFWorld
coordination study uses separate Qwen3.5-9B-class Engineer and Solver
actors with independent critics, initialized from Agent SFT, and
collects eight paired episodes per round for 144 rounds.

#### Baselines.

Except for locally evaluated JoMoHa and WHALE, scores are taken from
Harness-R1 ([Shao et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)); we use its training and
test sets, with checkpoint and harness selection on a separate
validation set. The task model is Qwen3.5-9B; frontier model names
denote harness editors, not replacement Solvers. Agent SFT + Harness-R1
additionally fine-tunes the task model, while WHALE uses its
RSFT-plus-search recipe. WHALE alternates after eight environment
interactions (16 training steps), uses the same harness-search settings
as JoMoHa, and matches its total environment-interaction budget.
Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")
examines one-sided learning, frozen-Engineer training, program swaps,
and coordination components.

### 6.1 Main Results

JoMoHa achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on
all three benchmarks: 97.0% on ALFWorld, 45.8% on WebShop, and 68.0% on
DBBench
(Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Schedule: give the Solver additional adaptation. ‣ 5.3 Coordinating Policy Updates ‣ 5 JoMoHa ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
Its average success is 70.3%, exceeding Agent SFT + Harness-R1 by 6.1
percentage points and WHALE by 7.2 points. The gains over WHALE are
16.5, 2.4, and 2.7 points across the three environments, respectively.

The ALFWorld breakdown locates the largest gains on tasks that transform
an object’s state before placement. Against the strongest competing
result in each category, JoMoHa gains 18.2 points on Clean, 17.3 on
Heat, and 24.8 on Cool, compared with 0.0–4.0 points on the remaining
categories. This pattern extends beyond differences in ceiling effects:
on Heat and Cool, the gains remove approximately 83.6% and 89.9% of the
respective best competitor’s errors . These tasks require execution to
distinguish a completed transformation from the remaining navigation and
placement, making the results consistent with the state-tracking issue
diagnosed in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Diagnosing Model–Harness Compatibility ‣ 4 Why Learn Weights and Harnesses Together? ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning").
Pick2 remains the weakest category at 91.8%, indicating remaining room
for improvement when multiple objects must be collected and placed.

### 6.2 Ablation Studies

We examine three sources of improvement: training the Engineer rather
than only resampling its outputs, improving the harness at fixed Solver
weights, and coordinating the two policies beyond the Joint-only
baseline.

#### Training the Engineer beyond fresh harness sampling.

Frozen Engineer fixes the initial Engineer parameters while continuing
to sample fresh harnesses and train the Solver. It reaches 90.5% at step
144, versus 97.0% for JoMoHa
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning"));
even its best reported checkpoint, 91.5% at step 108, remains 5.5 points
below the complete method. Thus, the gap persists when the control can
both resample programs and use its best reported checkpoint. Weight-only
and Harness-only reach 89.5% and 80.5%, respectively. Together, these
controls favor training both policies over the evaluated one-sided
recipes, while the component study below examines the additional benefit
of coordination.

#### Harness utility at unchanged Solver weights.

Learning curves alone cannot separate improvements in Solver ability
from improvements in the generated runtime. We therefore cross-evaluate
saved programs and Solver checkpoints
(Table [5](#S6.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 6.1 Main Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
At the later Solver, replacing the initial program with the later
program raises success from 92.5% to 96.5%, without changing model
weights. Relative to no harness, the later program gains 5.0 points,
with no observed success-to-failure regressions on this evaluation set.
The earlier and later learned programs also both improve the earlier
Solver from 91.5% under the initial program to 95.0%. These results show
that the saved programs contribute useful behavior beyond the initial
runtime, including at a different Solver checkpoint. The equal 95.0%
scores on the earlier Solver, but 95.0% versus 96.5% on the later
Solver, further show that program value depends on the Solver with which
it is paired.

#### Coordinating the two learners.

Joint-only trains both policies from paired task outcomes without
Context, ValueNorm, Peer, or Schedule. Adding each mechanism separately
raises its final success from 88.5% to 91.5–92.5%; combining all four
reaches 97.0%, an 8.5-point improvement over Joint-only
(Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 6.1 Main Results ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ JoMoHa: Joint Model–Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning")).
Context yields the highest single-addition point estimate, 92.5%,
consistent with the value of informing each critic about its
collaboration conditions. Schedule and Peer both achieve 92.0%, while
ValueNorm achieves 91.5%.

## 7 Discussion and Conclusion

One model learns to write the runtime; another learns to act under it.
JoMoHa trains both from the same task result while keeping their token
histories and value estimates separate. Fixed-component tests measure
the two sides of this interaction. At fixed Solver weights, saved
programs improve on the initial code. Learning the writer outperforms
freezing it while still sampling new code, and coordinating the two
learners improves on joint updates alone. The complete system has the
highest reported success on all three environments in the benchmark
table, averaging 70.3%. This is RSI through execution feedback: both the
task policy and the policy that constructs its runtime are learned
within the system.
````
